# 20.4.2 The Prime Subring; Subrings Generated by Elements

Every ring contains a canonical smallest subring, the **prime subring**, which captures the most intrinsic arithmetic of the ring. It is the subring generated by the multiplicative identity alone, and it is determined entirely by the characteristic. Understanding it requires revisiting the canonical map $\mathbb{Z} \to R$ from §20.3.3.

The prime subring of $R$ is the image of the unique ring homomorphism$\phi: \mathbb{Z} \to R$,$\phi(n) = n \cdot 1_R$. It is the subring generated by$1_R$ alone — the set of all$\mathbb{Z}$-multiples of the identity. When$\mathrm{char}(R) = 0$, this image is isomorphic to$\mathbb{Z}$, and the prime subring is a copy of the integers sitting inside$R$. When$\mathrm{char}(R) = p$, the image is isomorphic to$\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$, so the prime subring is a copy of the field$\mathbb{F}_p$. In either case, the prime subring is the smallest subring of$R$ in the sense that it is contained in every subring: any subring must contain$1_R$, hence all multiples of$1_R$.

The prime subring is canonical: any ring homomorphism $\phi: R \to S$ must send the prime subring of$R$ into the prime subring of$S$ (since$\phi(n \cdot 1_R) = n \cdot \phi(1_R) = n \cdot 1_S$). Ring homomorphisms are "compatible" with the prime subrings, which is one reason the prime subring is a fundamental invariant.

More generally, given any subset $A \subseteq R$, the **subring generated by$A$** is the smallest subring of$R$ containing$A$. It can be constructed as the intersection of all subrings of$R$ that contain$A$, and this intersection is again a subring (it contains$1_R$, is closed under subtraction and multiplication). Alternatively, one can describe it as the set of all ring-theoretic expressions in the elements of$A$: sums and products of elements of$A$ and their negatives, together with the identity$1_R$. This is the closure of$A \cup \{1_R\}$ under the ring operations.

When $A$ consists of a single element$\{a\}$, the generated subring is:
$$\mathbb{Z}[a] = \{c_0 \cdot 1_R + c_1 a + c_2 a^2 + \cdots + c_n a^n : c_i \in \mathbb{Z}, n \geq 0\}.$$
This is the set of polynomial expressions in $a$ with integer coefficients. If$R$ contains$\mathbb{Z}$ as its prime subring (i.e.,$\mathrm{char}(R) = 0$), then this is exactly the image of the evaluation map$\mathrm{ev}_a: \mathbb{Z}[x] \to R$,$f(x) \mapsto f(a)$. By the first isomorphism theorem:
$$\mathbb{Z}[a] \cong \mathbb{Z}[x] / \ker(\mathrm{ev}_a).$$
The kernel consists of all polynomials vanishing at $a$, which is either$\{0\}$ (if$a$ satisfies no polynomial relation over$\mathbb{Z}$) or a principal ideal$(f)$ for the minimal polynomial$f$ of$a$ over$\mathbb{Z}$.

This perspective — that the subring generated by an element is always a quotient of a polynomial ring — makes the polynomial ring the "free" commutative ring on one generator, and it will be made precise by the universal property of polynomial rings in Chapter 23.

**Example 1.** The prime subring of $\mathbb{C}$ is$\{n \cdot 1 : n \in \mathbb{Z}\} = \mathbb{Z}$ (realized as integer multiples of$1 \in \mathbb{C}$). Since$\mathrm{char}(\mathbb{C}) = 0$, this is isomorphic to$\mathbb{Z}$. The subring of$\mathbb{C}$ generated by$\{i\}$ is$\mathbb{Z}[i] = \{a + bi : a, b \in \mathbb{Z}\}$, the Gaussian integers. The evaluation map$\mathbb{Z}[x] \to \mathbb{C}$,$f \mapsto f(i)$, has kernel$(x^2 + 1)$ and image$\mathbb{Z}[i]$, so$\mathbb{Z}[i] \cong \mathbb{Z}[x]/(x^2 + 1)$.

**Example 2.** The prime subring of $\mathbb{F}_{p^n}$ is$\mathbb{F}_p$ (the field with$p$ elements). The full field$\mathbb{F}_{p^n}$ is generated over its prime subring by one element$\alpha$ (a primitive element, guaranteed to exist by the primitive element theorem). The minimal polynomial of$\alpha$ over$\mathbb{F}_p$ has degree$n$, so$\mathbb{F}_{p^n} \cong \mathbb{F}_p[x]/(f)$ for some irreducible$f \in \mathbb{F}_p[x]$ of degree$n$.

**Example 3.** The subring of $\mathbb{R}$ generated by$\{\sqrt{2}, \sqrt{3}\}$ is$\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{2}, \sqrt{3}]$. Its elements are polynomial expressions in$\sqrt{2}$ and$\sqrt{3}$. Since$\sqrt{2} \cdot \sqrt{3} = \sqrt{6}$ and$(\sqrt{2})^2 = 2$,$(\sqrt{3})^2 = 3$, the ring is spanned over$\mathbb{Z}$ by$\{1, \sqrt{2}, \sqrt{3}, \sqrt{6}\}$: every polynomial in$\sqrt{2}$ and$\sqrt{3}$ reduces to a$\mathbb{Z}$-linear combination of these four elements.

**Example 4.** The subring of $M_2(\mathbb{Q})$ generated by the single matrix$A = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ is the set$\{aI + bA : a, b \in \mathbb{Z}\}$. Note$A^2 = -I$, so$A^3 = -A$,$A^4 = I$, and the pattern repeats with period$4$. Higher powers of$A$ reduce to$\pm I$ and$\pm A$, so the generated subring has$\mathbb{Z}$-basis$\{I, A\}$ and is isomorphic to$\mathbb{Z}[x]/(x^2 + 1) \cong \mathbb{Z}[i]$.

**Example 5.** For a commutative ring $R$ and elements$a_1, \ldots, a_k$, the subring$R_0 = \mathbb{Z}[a_1, \ldots, a_k]$ generated by these elements is the image of the evaluation map$\mathbb{Z}[x_1, \ldots, x_k] \to R$ sending$x_i \mapsto a_i$. This map's kernel consists of all polynomial relations satisfied by$a_1, \ldots, a_k$ with integer coefficients, and the quotient is$\mathbb{Z}[a_1, \ldots, a_k]$. The structure of this subring — whether it is a domain, a PID, has finite dimension over$\mathbb{Z}$ — encodes the arithmetic relations among the$a_i$.
